title: Compound Interest: Why Your Money Grows Faster Over Time
audience: Adults who can do basic arithmetic (including percentages) and have a savings account, but have never learned the compound interest formula.

objectives.text: Learner can explain that compound interest pays interest on past interest, not just on the original deposit.
Learner can compute a balance after several years using A = P × (1 + r)^n.
Learner can explain why growth speeds up over time and compare savers who start at different times.

blocks.markdown:
Your bank pays you **interest**, a percentage of your balance.

With **simple interest**, you only earn on the money you first put in. $1,000 at 10% earns $100 every year, always.

With **compound interest**, the interest is added to your balance. Next year you earn interest on that bigger balance. So **your interest starts earning interest too.**

- Year 1: 10% of $1,000 = $100. Balance: $1,100.
- Year 2: 10% of $1,100 = $110. Balance: $1,210.

The extra $10 in year 2 is interest earned on last year's interest. Most savings accounts work this way. Real accounts often compound monthly or daily. This lesson uses yearly compounding to keep the math simple.

item.stem: You put **$1,000** in an account that pays **10% a year, compounded**. After year 1 your balance is $1,100. How much interest do you earn **during year 2**?

choices.feedback: Right. The bank pays 10% of your current balance, $1,100. That's $110.
That's simple interest, where you only earn on the original $1,000. With compounding, last year's $100 is now part of your balance and earns interest too.
choices.misconception: Thinks interest is always calculated on the original deposit (simple interest).

choices.feedback: $210 is the total interest over both years ($100 + $110). The question asks only about year 2.
choices.misconception: Mixes up one year's interest with the total interest so far.

choices.feedback: That's your balance after year 2, not the interest earned during year 2. Subtract the $1,100 you started the year with.
choices.misconception: Confuses the end-of-year balance with the interest earned that year.

blocks.markdown:
Each year you multiply your balance by **(1 + r)**, where r is the rate as a decimal. At 10%, that's × 1.10.

Over **n** years you multiply n times. That gives the formula:

**A = P × (1 + r)^n**

- **P** = what you put in (the principal)
- **r** = yearly rate as a decimal (5% → 0.05)
- **n** = number of years
- **A** = what you end up with

The `^n` means "multiply (1 + r) by itself n times", e.g. 1.10^3 = 1.10 × 1.10 × 1.10. A calculator's `^` or `xʸ` key does this for you.

blocks.problem: You deposit **$1,000** at **5%** a year, compounded yearly. What is the balance after **3 years**?
steps: Write down the pieces: P = 1000, r = 5% = **0.05**, n = **3**.
Sanity check: simple interest would give $1,150 ($50 × 3). Compounding gives $7.63 more. That's the interest on your interest.

item.stem: You deposit **$2,000** at **4%** a year, compounded yearly. What is the balance after **2 years**? (Round to the nearest cent.)
item.feedbackWrong: Got **2,160**? That's simple interest (2000 × 1.08). Got **163.20**? That's only the interest; include the $2,000. Otherwise: square 1.04, then multiply by 2000.

blocks.hint: P = 2000, r = 0.04 (not 4), n = 2. The 2 is an exponent: 1.04^2 means 1.04 × 1.04, not 1.04 × 2.

item.stem: You leave **$5,000** in an account at **6%** a year for **10 years**, compounded yearly. What is the final balance? (Round to the nearest dollar.)
item.feedbackCorrect: Right, about $8,954. Simple interest would give only $8,000. Compounding added about $954 more.
item.feedbackWrong: Got **8,000**? That's simple interest (0.06 × 10 = 0.6). Got **3,954**? That's the interest only; add back the $5,000. Otherwise, raise 1.06 to the 10th power, then multiply by 5,000.

blocks.hint: Use A = P × (1 + r)^n with P = 5000, r = 0.06, n = 10. Use your calculator's ^ key for 1.06^10.

blocks.problem: Both earn **6%** a year. **Ana** invests $1,000 at age 25. **Ben** invests $1,000 at age 35. Neither adds more. How much does each have at 65?
steps: Ana's money grows for **40 years**. Ben's grows for **30 years**.
Ben started just 10 years later, yet he ends with only a little over **half** of what Ana has.
Same rate, same deposit. The only difference is how long the money had to compound. Why do 10 years matter that much? The next activity shows you.

blocks.prompt:
The curve shows **$1,000** growing over the years (x-axis) at the rate you choose.

Set the rate to **8%**. The curve will pass through the two markers. Compare how much it rises from **year 0 to 5** with how much it rises from **year 30 to 35**. Does each 5 years add the same amount?

blocks.markdown:
You just saw it. The same 8% added about 10 times more dollars late in the curve than early on.

That's because each year's interest is a percentage of a balance that keeps growing. So the money doesn't grow in a straight line. It **curves upward**, and it gets steeper the longer you wait.

That's why **time is often the most powerful ingredient**. The early years feel slow. The late years do most of the work. That's also why Ben fell so far behind Ana.

A handy shortcut is the **Rule of 72**. Divide 72 by the rate (in %) to estimate how many years it takes your money to double.

At 6%, 72 ÷ 6 = about **12 years** to double. At 8%, 72 ÷ 8 = about **9 years**.

After it doubles once, it doubles again in the same number of years. That's why waiting longer pays off so much.

blocks.prompt:
Same curve: **$1,000** growing at the rate you choose.

Use the Rule of 72 to guess a rate that makes $1,000 **double to about $2,000 in 10 years**. Then set it and see whether the curve hits the marker.

goal.description: Set the rate so the balance after 10 years is about $2,000 (double the start).
goal.feedbackSuccess: About 7% doubles your money in 10 years, just as the Rule of 72 predicts (72 ÷ 7 ≈ 10). Look at year 40: the money has doubled about 4 times, to roughly $15,000.

item.stem: You invest **$1,000 at 7%** and add nothing more. Which decade adds more dollars to your balance?

choices.feedback: Right. Years 1–10 add about $970 (to about $1,970). Years 31–40 add about $7,360 (from about $7,610 to about $14,970). The same 7% is applied to a much bigger balance.

choices.text: Both add the same, because the rate is the same
choices.feedback: The rate is the same, but it's applied to a growing balance. 7% of $7,600 is far more than 7% of $1,000. So the dollars added each decade keep growing.
choices.misconception: Thinks compound growth is linear: same rate means the same dollar amount each year.

choices.text: Years 1–10, because that's when the money starts growing
choices.feedback: Starting early matters because it gives the money more time, but the early years themselves add the least. Each decade adds more than the one before.
choices.misconception: Confuses 'starting early is important' with 'the early years add the most money'.

choices.text: Both add the same, because the balance about doubles in each decade
choices.feedback: Both decades do double the balance. But doubling $1,000 adds about $1,000, while doubling $7,600 adds about $7,600. The same doubling means far more dollars later.
choices.misconception: Mixes up the same growth factor (doubling) with the same number of dollars added.

blocks.hint: Look at the 7% curve you just made. How much does it rise between years 0 and 10, and between years 30 and 40?

blocks.prompt: Use the Rule of 72 to find the rate that doubles $1,000 in **8 years**, then check it on the curve. Does it pass close to the marker?

goal.description: Set the rate so $1,000 reaches about $2,000 at year 8.
goal.feedbackSuccess: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, so 9% it is. At 9%, $1,000 grows to about $1,993 in 8 years, very close to double. The curve then doubles again by year 16 (about $4,000) and again by year 24 (about $8,000).

item.stem: Both earn **7%** a year until age 65. **Ana** invests **$1,000 at age 25**. **Ben** invests **$1,500 at age 35**. Who has more at 65?

choices.feedback: Yes. Ana's money doubles about 4 times (≈ $14,970). Ben's doubles about 3 times (≈ $11,420). Ten extra years of compounding beat Ben's extra $500.

choices.text: Ben, because he put in more money
choices.feedback: A bigger deposit helps, but Ana's extra 10 years give her one more doubling. That's worth far more than Ben's extra $500.
choices.misconception: Thinks the size of the deposit matters more than how long it compounds.

choices.text: About the same, since the rate is the same
choices.feedback: Same rate doesn't mean the same result. The number of years is in the exponent, so 10 more years makes a big difference.
choices.misconception: Thinks the rate alone decides the outcome and ignores time.

choices.text: Ben, because each year adds about the same amount, so Ana's extra 10 years add only about $700
choices.feedback: That's straight-line (simple interest) thinking. With compounding, each year adds more than the last, and the final years add the most. Ana's extra 10 years give her a whole extra doubling, not just $700.
choices.misconception: Thinks compound growth is linear, the same dollar amount each year.

blocks.hint: At 7%, money roughly doubles every 10 years. Count the doublings for each person.

points: Compound interest pays interest on your interest, not just on what you put in.
Formula: A = P × (1 + r)^n. Write the rate as a decimal and raise (1 + r) to the number of years.
Each year's interest is bigger than the last, so growth curves upward and speeds up over time. At 8%, years 30–35 added 10 times more than years 0–5.
Rule of 72: 72 ÷ rate ≈ years to double your money. You checked it yourself at 7% and 9%.
Starting earlier often beats putting in more later, because time is in the exponent.
